# The apply family to iterators {#sec-iterators}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

R gives you two ways to work on every element of a vector without writing a loop: vectorized functions such as `x * 2`, and the apply family (`lapply()`, `sapply()`, `vapply()`, `Map()`, `Filter()`, and `Reduce()`), which call a function on each element. Rust's equivalent is the *iterator*, a value that hands out elements one at a time, with methods such as `map()`, `filter()`, and `sum()` that chain into a pipeline. This chapter maps the apply family onto iterator methods. It also finishes several examples that earlier chapters left for later: a shorter doubling loop and selecting elements by position (@sec-vectors), counting matches (@sec-types), and collecting the pieces of a split string (@sec-strings). The matching section of the Rust book is "Processing a Series of Items with Iterators" [@rustbook, sec. 13.2].

## From a loop to `map()`

@sec-vectors doubled a vector with a loop and `push()`. In R, `x * 2` or `sapply()` does it without a loop, and in Rust an iterator does it in one line:

```{r}
#| label: r-map
x <- c(10, 20, 30)
x * 2
sapply(x, function(v) v * 2)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-map
let v = vec![10, 20, 30];
// Each x is an &i32, and arithmetic works on a reference without *
let doubled: Vec<i32> = v.iter().map(|x| x * 2).collect();
println!("{:?}", doubled);
```

The chain has three steps:

- `v.iter()` creates an iterator that lends out each element of `v` in turn, as a reference (@sec-borrowing).
- `.map(|x| x * 2)` applies a function to each element. `|x| x * 2` is a *closure*, Rust's anonymous function: the arguments go between the vertical bars and the body follows. It's the counterpart of R's `function(v) v * 2`, or `\(v) v * 2` since R 4.1.0. @sec-closures covers what else closures can do.
- `.collect()` gathers the results into a collection. It can build several kinds, so it needs to be told which. Here the type on `doubled`, `Vec<i32>`, tells it. Leave the type off, and the compiler stops with "type annotations needed". The turbofish from @sec-generics works too: `.collect::<Vec<i32>>()`.

## Iterators are lazy

An iterator does nothing until something asks it for values. Here the closure prints each time it runs:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-lazy
let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let doubled = v.iter().map(|x| {
    println!("doubling {x}");
    x * 2
});
println!("nothing has run yet");
let result: Vec<i32> = doubled.collect();
println!("{:?}", result);
```

Calling `map()` only describes the work. The closure runs when `collect()` asks for the values, one element at a time. A `for` loop, `sum()`, and `count()` also ask for values; an iterator that nothing consumes never runs, and the compiler warns about one.

Consuming an iterator uses it up. Here `collect()` takes ownership of `doubled`, so the iterator can't be used again, but `v` is still there, because `iter()` only borrowed it. A second pass needs a new iterator from `v.iter()`.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's apply functions run as soon as they're called and return the whole result. R is lazy in a different way: a function's arguments aren't evaluated until the function uses them (@sec-closures). An iterator's laziness is about the steps of a pipeline. Because each element passes through every step before the next element starts, a chain of `map()` and `filter()` builds no intermediate vectors, where `sapply()` followed by `Filter()` builds one.
:::

## Borrowing, changing, or consuming

The ownership rules of Part III decide how a vector can be iterated over, and there are three methods for the three cases:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-iter-kinds
let mut v = vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0];

for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = *x * 10.0;
}
println!("{:?}", v);

let total: f64 = v.iter().sum();
println!("{total}");

let halves: Vec<f64> = v.into_iter().map(|x| x / 2.0).collect();
println!("{:?}", halves);
```

The loop uses `iter_mut()`, which lends out each element as a mutable reference, so the loop can change it in place with `*x` (@sec-borrowing). Next, `iter()` lends out shared references, and `sum()` adds them up. Last, `into_iter()` takes ownership of the vector and hands out the elements themselves, so `v` can't be used afterward. A `for` loop picks one of these from how the vector is written:

| Method | Each element arrives as | Same as | The vector afterward |
|--------------|--------------|--------------|------------------------|
| `v.iter()` | `&T` | `for x in &v` | Unchanged |
| `v.iter_mut()` | `&mut T` | `for x in &mut v` | Possibly changed |
| `v.into_iter()` | `T` | `for x in v` | Moved; can't be used |

## `vapply()` and the type of the result

In R, `sapply()` and `vapply()` both apply a function to each element of a list. Here the list holds S3 normal distributions from @sec-s3-traits:

```{r}
#| label: r-vapply
normal <- function(mean = 0, sd = 1) {
  structure(list(mean = mean, sd = sd), class = "normal")
}
variance <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("variance")
variance.normal <- function(x, ...) x$sd^2

dists <- list(normal(0, 1), normal(5, 2), normal(-1, 0.5))
sapply(dists, variance)
vapply(dists, variance, numeric(1))
```

In Rust, `map()` calls the method on each distribution. The `Normal` is the one from @sec-s7, compiled but not shown, so each value comes from `new()`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-map-method
# mod distributions {
#     pub trait Distribution {
#         fn mean(&self) -> f64;
#         fn variance(&self) -> f64;
#     }
#
#     pub struct Normal {
#         mean: f64,
#         sd: f64,
#     }
#
#     impl Normal {
#         pub fn new(mean: f64, sd: f64) -> Result<Normal, String> {
#             if sd > 0.0 {
#                 Ok(Normal { mean, sd })
#             } else {
#                 Err(format!("sd must be positive, not {sd}"))
#             }
#         }
#     }
#
#     impl Distribution for Normal {
#         fn mean(&self) -> f64 {
#             self.mean
#         }
#
#         fn variance(&self) -> f64 {
#             self.sd * self.sd
#         }
#     }
# }
#
# use distributions::{Distribution, Normal};
#
fn main() {
    let dists = vec![
        Normal::new(0.0, 1.0).expect("valid parameters"),
        Normal::new(5.0, 2.0).expect("valid parameters"),
        Normal::new(-1.0, 0.5).expect("valid parameters"),
    ];
    let variances: Vec<f64> = dists.iter().map(|d| d.variance()).collect();
    println!("{:?}", variances);
}
```

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
The third argument of `vapply()`, `FUN.VALUE`, is a type annotation. Here `numeric(1)` says that each result is a single double, and `vapply()` checks every result against it:

```{r}
#| label: r-vapply-checks
#| error: true
sapply(list(), variance)
vapply(list(), variance, numeric(1))
vapply(1:3, function(i) letters[i], numeric(1))
```

With an empty input, `sapply()` gives back an empty list rather than an empty numeric vector, because it guesses the shape of its result from the values. By contrast, `vapply()` always returns what `FUN.VALUE` promised and stops when a result doesn't match. It does promote a logical or integer result to a double. The type `Vec<f64>` on `variances` is the same promise, checked when the program compiles, with no promotion: a closure that returned an integer or text would make `collect()` fail to compile. An integer needs an explicit conversion, `f64::from()` or, for a `usize`, `as f64` (@sec-types).
:::

## Filtering, counting, and selecting

R selects elements with a logical index or with `Filter()`, counts matches by summing a logical vector, and picks elements by position with an index vector. Rust does each with an iterator:

```{r}
#| label: r-filter
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
x[x > 15]
Filter(function(v) v > 15, x)
sum(x > 15)
x[c(1, 3)]
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-filter
let v = vec![10, 20, 30, 40];

let big: Vec<i32> = v.iter().copied().filter(|x| *x > 15).collect();
println!("{:?}", big);

let n = v.iter().copied().filter(|x| *x > 15).count();
println!("{n}");

// R's c(1, 3), counting from 0; they're usize because they index v
let positions = vec![0, 2];
// Each i is an &usize, and indexing needs the usize itself, *i
let picked: Vec<i32> = positions.iter().map(|i| v[*i]).collect();
println!("{:?}", picked);
```

The `copied()` method turns an iterator over `&i32` into one over `i32`, copying each number as it passes, which works for any `Copy` type (@sec-ownership). Then `filter()` keeps the elements for which the closure returns `true`. It lends each element to the closure as a reference, because it only needs to look at it, so `x` is an `&i32` and `*x` is the number. In the second chain, `count()` counts what's left; @sec-types pointed out that Rust can't count with `sum()` because a `bool` isn't a number. The last chain is R's `x[c(1, 3)]`: it maps each position to the element there.

The two R forms of selection differ when `x` has a missing value: `x[x > 15]` keeps an `NA` where the comparison is `NA`, and `Filter()` drops it. A `Vec<i32>` can't hold a missing value (@sec-missingness), so the Rust chain has no missing values to keep or drop.

## `Reduce()` and `fold()`

In R, `Reduce()` combines the elements one at a time with a two-argument function. Rust's `fold()` does the same, starting from a value you supply, like `Reduce()` with its `init` argument:

```{r}
#| label: r-reduce
x <- c(2.5, 9, 4)
sum(x)
Reduce(function(acc, v) acc * v, x, 1)
max(x)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-fold
let v = vec![2.5, 9.0, 4.0];

let total: f64 = v.iter().sum();
println!("{total}");

let product = v.iter().fold(1.0, |acc, x| acc * x);
println!("{product}");

// x is an &f64: the product uses it without *, but max() needs *x
let largest = v.iter().fold(f64::NEG_INFINITY, |acc, x| acc.max(*x));
println!("{largest}");
```

Like `collect()`, `sum()` needs the type of its result, given here on `total`. The closure passed to `fold()` takes the running value and the next element and returns the new running value.

The last `fold()` stands in for R's `max()`. Iterators have a `max()` method, but it doesn't compile for `f64`: it requires a type whose values can always be put in order, and `NaN` can't be (@sec-missingness). Starting from negative infinity and keeping the larger value at each step gives the largest number instead.

The fold isn't quite R's `max()`, though. When one argument is `NaN`, `f64::max()` returns the other [@rust-std], so the fold skips `NaN` values, where `max()` in R returns `NaN`. It behaves like `max(x, na.rm = TRUE)`, down to the result for a vector with no numbers in it: both give negative infinity, and R also warns.

## `Map()` and `zip()`

In R, `Map()` walks through two vectors in step, and Rust pairs them with `zip()`. Here the second vector is one element longer:

```{r}
#| label: r-map-two
Map(function(a, b) a + b, 1:3, 4:7)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-zip
let a = vec![1, 2, 3];
let b = vec![4, 5, 6, 7];
let sums: Vec<i32> = a.iter().zip(b.iter()).map(|(x, y)| x + y).collect();
println!("{:?}", sums);
```

R recycles the shorter vector, adding 1 and 7 for a fourth result, and warns because 4 isn't a multiple of 3. In Rust, `zip()` produces pairs, and the closure's `(x, y)` takes each pair apart, the same pattern as matching on pairs in @sec-enums. The pairs stop at the end of the shorter input, so the 7 is ignored without a warning. Rust has no recycling; it leaves the decision to you, as @sec-vectors said.

## `seq_along()` and `enumerate()`

A loop that needs each element's position uses `seq_along()` in R and `enumerate()` in Rust:

```{r}
#| label: r-enumerate
x <- c(10, 20, 30)
for (i in seq_along(x)) {
  cat(i, ": ", x[i], "\n", sep = "")
}
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-enumerate
let v = vec![10, 20, 30];
for (i, value) in v.iter().enumerate() {
    println!("{i}: {value}");
}
```

The `enumerate()` method pairs each element with its position. It counts from zero, so Rust prints positions 0 to 2 where R prints 1 to 3.

## Collecting other things

Collecting isn't limited to vectors of numbers. @sec-strings split a string with a `for` loop over the pieces; in Rust, collecting them gives the counterpart of R's `strsplit()`:

```{r}
#| label: r-strsplit
strsplit("a,b,c", ",")[[1]]
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-split-collect
let parts: Vec<&str> = "a,b,c".split(",").collect();
println!("{:?}", parts);
```

Each piece is a `&str` that borrows from the original string, so no text is copied. @sec-collections collects into other collections, such as sets.

::: {.callout-note title="An R habit to drop in Rust"}
In R, a loop is often the slow way to do something a vectorized function does quickly, so R programmers learn to avoid loops. In Rust, an iterator chain and the equivalent loop run at about the same speed in an optimized build (@sec-setup). The Rust book calls iterators one of Rust's zero-cost abstractions, because they compile to roughly the same code as the loop you'd write yourself [@rustbook, sec. 13.4]. A debug build, like the ones in this book, skips that optimization and can run the iterator slower. Choose whichever reads better, and time the code if its speed matters.
:::

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `sapply(x, f)`, `lapply(x, f)` | `v.iter().map(f).collect()` |
| `function(v) v * 2`, `\(v) v * 2` | `|x| x * 2` |
| Apply functions run at once | Iterators run when consumed |
| `for (x in v)`: changing `x` leaves `v` alone | `iter()`, `iter_mut()`, `into_iter()`: borrow, change, or take the elements |
| `vapply(x, f, numeric(1))` | `let y: Vec<f64> = ...collect();` |
| `x[x > 15]`, `Filter(f, x)` | `.filter(|x| ...)` |
| `sum(x > 15)` | `.filter(...).count()` |
| `x[c(1, 3)]` | `positions.iter().map(|i| v[*i])` |
| `Reduce(f, x, init)` | `.fold(init, |acc, x| ...)` |
| `Map(f, x, y)` | `x.iter().zip(y.iter()).map(...)` |
| `seq_along(x)` | `.enumerate()` |
| `strsplit(s, ",")[[1]]` | `s.split(",").collect()` |
| Loops are often slow; vectorize | Iterators run about as fast as loops in optimized builds |
